title: Filter employees who joined after 2015 and belong to the "IT" department.
shortTitle: Filter employees who joined after 2015 and belong to the "IT" department

s1_definition.profdef: Combining conditions in a `filter` means supplying a predicate built from a logical AND of two tests, so an element survives only when both are true. You can either write one lambda with the double ampersand operator, or chain two `filter` calls, which is logically equivalent for an AND.
s1_definition.analogy: The HR manager at the National Bank of India now has two rules at the door: "You must be in the IT department AND you must have joined after 2015." s1_definition.oneliner: Use logical AND inside one predicate (or chain filters) so an element survives only when every condition is true.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Combining conditions in a `filter` means supplying a predicate built from a logical AND of two tests, so an element survives only when both are true. You can either write one lambda with the double ampersand operator, or chain two `filter` calls, which is logically equivalent for an AND.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The HR manager at the National Bank of India now has two rules at the door: "You must be in the IT department AND you must have joined after 2015." Rajesh joined IT in 2018 and walks straight through; someone who joined IT back in 2010 is stopped because he fails the second rule. Both rules must say yes.

**One line to remember:** Use logical AND inside one predicate (or chain filters) so an element survives only when every condition is true.

sections.s2_technical:
A predicate is any function returning a boolean. To require two things at once you combine them with the logical AND operator, for example `e -> e.getDepartment().equals("IT") && e.getJoinYear() > 2015`. Java short-circuits the AND, so if the department check fails the year check is never evaluated, which is a small performance win and also avoids unnecessary work.

You can also use the `Predicate` combinator methods. If you define `Predicate<Employee> isIt = e -> e.getDepartment().equals("IT");` and `Predicate<Employee> joinedRecently = e -> e.getJoinYear() > 2015;`, then `isIt.and(joinedRecently)` produces a combined predicate. This is cleaner when the conditions are reused across the codebase and reads almost like English.

Chaining `stream.filter(isIt).filter(joinedRecently)` gives the same result as a single ANDed predicate, because an element must survive the first filter to even reach the second. For a strict year comparison, "after 2015" means strictly greater than 2015, so 2015 itself does not qualify — a common off-by-one trap in interviews.

A senior nuance: use the equals method for the department String, never the double-equals reference comparison, because reference comparison would fail for equal-but-distinct String objects. Guarding against a null department is also wise in real data.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India is giving a loyalty-and-skills certificate to its newer technology staff. The rule from the CTO is precise: the employee must be in the IT department and must have joined after 2015, because the certificate recognises people hired during the bank's digital transformation. HR has a mixed list across all departments and all joining years. We must pick exactly the people who satisfy both rules. This is exactly how a combined predicate works — each employee is tested against department equals IT and join year greater than 2015, and only those passing both are selected.

The code adds a `joinYear` field to the `Employee` class. An `EligibilityService` exposes `recentItStaff(List<Employee>)`. It builds two reusable predicates and combines them with `and`, then filters and collects. The runnable `Main` feeds a mixed list and logs the selected certificate recipients.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (IT, 2018), Vikram (IT, 2010), Priya (Sales, 2019), Neha (IT, 2021).

Step 1: `staff.stream()` opens the pipeline over four employees.

Step 2: Rajesh enters. Department equals IT is true; join year 2018 greater than 2015 is true. Both true, so Rajesh passes.

Step 3: Vikram enters. Department IT is true, but join year 2010 is not greater than 2015, so the AND is false and Vikram is dropped. Short-circuiting means once the year fails the result is decided.

Step 4: Priya enters. Department equals IT is false immediately, so the AND short-circuits and Priya is dropped without even checking the year.

Step 5: Neha enters. IT is true and 2021 greater than 2015 is true, so Neha passes.

Step 6: `collect` gathers Rajesh and Neha into a new list.

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I need two conditions at once, I combine them into a single predicate using logical AND, so an element survives the filter only when both tests are true. I can write it inline as one lambda with the double ampersand operator, or I can define two named predicates and join them with the predicate combinator method called and, which reads almost like plain English and lets me reuse each rule elsewhere in the codebase.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this came up when the CTO asked for a loyalty certificate for technology staff hired during the digital transformation. The rule was precise: the employee had to be in the IT department and must have joined after 2015. I built one predicate for the department check and another for the join year, combined them with and, and filtered the employee stream. I was careful that "after 2015" means strictly greater than 2015, so someone who joined in 2015 itself does not qualify — that off-by-one is a classic trap.

A senior point I add is that Java short-circuits the AND, so if the department check fails the year check is never even evaluated, which avoids wasted work. I also always compare the department String with the equals method rather than the double-equals reference comparison, because reference comparison would silently fail for two equal but distinct String objects, and in production banking data that would quietly drop valid employees. Composing small named predicates also keeps the code open for extension — if finance later adds a third rule, I just write one more predicate and chain it on.

---

keyPoints: Uses filter() with a Predicate<T> to select matching elements
Lazy operation — no processing until terminal operation
Can chain multiple filters or use complex Predicate with && ||
